topic: Waves in air, fluids and solids: Properties of waves
subject: physics

items.q: A transverse wave is drawn with its undisturbed position shown as a horizontal centre line. What is the amplitude of this wave?
items.correct: The maximum displacement of a point on the wave from its undisturbed position
items.misconception: The vertical distance from the bottom of a trough up to the top of a crest
items.why: The crest-to-trough distance is the most visually obvious measurement on a diagram, and everyday language calls that the height of a wave. The undisturbed line is often faint or missing, so students measure between the two features they can actually see. Find the undisturbed centre line first and measure from there. Crest to trough is twice the amplitude, so a wave whose crests are 3 cm above the line has an amplitude of 3 cm, not 6 cm.
items.random_wrong: The displacement of a point on the wave at the instant it is measured

items.q: Which distance on a wave diagram is exactly one wavelength?
items.correct: From a point on one wave to the equivalent point on the adjacent wave
items.misconception: From the top of a crest to the bottom of the trough next to it
items.why: A crest and the next trough are neighbouring features, and the gap between them looks like one complete piece of the pattern. Students match adjacent features rather than equivalent ones. The two points must be equivalent, not merely adjacent: crest to crest, or trough to trough. Crest to the next trough is half a wavelength, so doubling it gives λ.
items.random_wrong: From the first crest drawn on the diagram to the very last crest drawn

items.q: What does the frequency of a wave tell you?
items.correct: The number of waves passing a point each second
items.misconception: The speed at which a wave moves through the medium
items.why: In everyday speech a high frequency sounds like something happening fast, and both quantities involve 'per second'. Students hear 'high frequency' and picture a wave racing along. Frequency counts waves per second at a fixed point; speed measures distance travelled per second. Two waves in the same medium travel at the same speed however different their frequencies are.
items.random_wrong: The number of complete waves drawn on the diagram

items.q: Ripples pass a floating cork. Which statement is correct?
items.correct: The period is the time one whole ripple takes to pass
items.misconception: The frequency is the speed at which the ripples travel
items.why: In everyday speech a high frequency sounds like something happening fast, and both quantities involve 'per second'. Students hear 'high frequency' and picture a wave racing along. Frequency counts waves per second at a fixed point; speed measures distance travelled per second. Two waves in the same medium travel at the same speed however different their frequencies are.
items.random_wrong: The amplitude is the cork's displacement at any instant

items.q: A wave has a frequency of 8 Hz. What is its period?
items.misconception: 8 s
items.why: Both quantities describe the timing of the same wave and are often introduced in the same breath, so students treat them as interchangeable and simply carry the number across. They are reciprocals, not equals. A large frequency means a small period: eight waves each second means each one takes an eighth of a second.

items.q: A wave has a period of 0.004 s. Using [T = 1/f], what is its frequency?
items.correct: 250 Hz
items.misconception: 25 Hz
items.why: Reciprocals of small whole numbers are done mentally and the place value slips, especially when a calculator is not used and the digits 1, 2, 5 or 8 appear. Check the size of the answer: eight waves each second means each one lasts well under a second, so 0.125 s is sensible and 1.25 s cannot be right.
items.random_wrong: 4 Hz

items.q: Which statement about the period of a wave is correct?
items.correct: It is measured in seconds, because it is a time
items.misconception: It is measured in hertz, the same unit as the frequency
items.why: Period and frequency are linked by one equation and taught together, so the unit attaches itself to the wrong quantity. Hertz is the newer, more memorable unit and gets applied to both. Hertz counts events each second, so it belongs to frequency. Period is a length of time, so it is measured in seconds.
items.random_wrong: It is measured in waves per second, like the frequency

items.q: In one second, 400 complete waves pass a point. How should this be recorded?
items.correct: 400 Hz, because 400 waves pass each second
items.misconception: 400 s, because the waves are counted over a second
items.why: The definition of frequency contains the word 'second', so students attach the second as the unit rather than recognising it as part of a rate. The second in the definition is the time over which the waves are counted, not the unit of the answer. A count each second is measured in hertz.
items.random_wrong: 0.0025 Hz, because frequency is one over 400

items.q: What is meant by the wave speed?
items.correct: The speed at which the energy is transferred through the medium
items.misconception: The speed at which particles of the medium move up and down
items.why: Diagrams and animations show particles oscillating, and that is the visible motion. Students see moving particles and assume the wave is those particles travelling. The particles oscillate about fixed undisturbed positions and go nowhere overall; a floating cork bobs but is not carried to the shore. What travels is the energy, and its speed is the wave speed.
items.random_wrong: The number of complete waves that pass a point each second

items.q: Which statement about the wave equation is correct?
items.correct: It applies to all waves, transverse and longitudinal
items.misconception: It applies only to transverse waves, such as water ripples
items.why: Wavelength and amplitude are first taught on a drawn transverse wave, so the equation feels tied to that picture. Longitudinal compressions look nothing like the diagram. The specification states that all waves obey the wave equation. A longitudinal wave still has a wavelength — compression to the next compression — and a frequency, so v = f λ applies unchanged.
items.random_wrong: It applies to light waves but not to sound waves

items.q: How is the wave speed related to the frequency and the wavelength?
items.correct: The wave speed is the frequency times the wavelength
items.misconception: The wave speed is the frequency divided by the wavelength
items.why: Students remember that the three quantities are linked but not how. Speed formulas met earlier, such as speed = distance ÷ time, are divisions, so division is assumed here too. Check the units: Hz is 'per second' and λ is in metres, so multiplying gives metres per second. Dividing would give per-second-per-metre, which is not a speed.
items.random_wrong: The wave speed is the frequency added to the wavelength

items.q: The wave equation is [v = f λ]. Which rearrangement correctly gives the wavelength?
items.correct: λ = v / f, the speed divided by the frequency
items.misconception: λ = f / v, the frequency divided by the wave speed
items.why: Students remember that the three quantities are linked but not how. Speed formulas met earlier, such as speed = distance ÷ time, are divisions, so division is assumed here too. Check the units: Hz is 'per second' and λ is in metres, so multiplying gives metres per second. Dividing would give per-second-per-metre, which is not a speed.
items.random_wrong: λ = v f, the speed multiplied by the frequency

items.q: A student uses [v = f λ] with the frequency in hertz and the wavelength in metres. What unit does the calculated wave speed have?
items.correct: Metres per second, m/s, since the answer is a speed
items.misconception: Hertz, Hz, the unit taken from the frequency
items.why: Students substitute numbers and copy a unit from the question rather than thinking about what the calculated quantity is. The equation has no obvious 'speed' symbol to prompt them. The unit follows the quantity being found. The specification gives wave speed, v, in metres per second, m/s, and multiplying per-second by metres does produce metres per second.
items.random_wrong: Metres, m, the unit taken from the wavelength

items.q: A sound wave has a frequency of 2.5 kHz. What is this frequency in hertz?
items.why: Unit conversions are remembered as 'move the decimal point by three' without a check on direction, and many conversions students meet do involve dividing. A kilohertz is bigger than a hertz, so there must be more hertz in the answer, not fewer. Multiply by 1000 when going from kHz to Hz.
items.random_wrong: 250 Hz

items.q: Ripples on a tank have a wavelength of 40 cm and a frequency of 5 Hz. What is their wave speed?
items.correct: 2 m/s
items.why: The number in the question is used exactly as printed, and centimetres feel like a perfectly ordinary unit of length, so no conversion seems necessary. The specification gives wavelength, λ, in metres, m. Any wavelength in cm or mm must be converted before substituting, or the speed comes out a hundred or a thousand times too large.

items.q: A wave is shown on a graph of displacement against distance. How are the amplitude and the wavelength read from it?
items.correct: Amplitude is vertical, wavelength is horizontal
items.misconception: Amplitude runs from a trough up to the crest above it
items.why: The crest-to-trough distance is the most visually obvious measurement on a diagram, and everyday language calls that the height of a wave. The undisturbed line is often faint or missing, so students measure between the two features they can actually see. Find the undisturbed centre line first and measure from there. Crest to trough is twice the amplitude, so a wave whose crests are 3 cm above the line has an amplitude of 3 cm, not 6 cm.
items.random_wrong: Both are measured along the horizontal distance axis

items.q: A class measures the speed of sound in air. Which method gives the most reliable value?
items.correct: Time the echo of a clap from a wall a measured distance away
items.misconception: Use a stopwatch to time a clap crossing the laboratory
items.why: Stopwatch-and-ruler is the standard recipe for speed in earlier work on moving objects, and sound is invisible, so students do not appreciate how quickly it crosses a room. Sound covers a classroom in about a hundredth of a second, while reaction time is about a fifth of a second. Use tens of metres, an echo, or electronic timing with two microphones.
items.random_wrong: Measure how loud the clap is at two different distances

items.q: In the echo method for the speed of sound, the distance to the wall is measured but twice that distance is used in the calculation. Why?
items.correct: Because the sound travels to the wall and back before it is heard
items.misconception: Because the wall creates a new wave that travels more slowly
items.why: Echoes are quieter than the original sound, and students associate less energy with less speed, so the returning sound is imagined as a fresh, feebler wave. Only the amplitude is reduced by reflection; the speed depends on the medium and is unchanged, which is why the echo method works at all.
items.random_wrong: Because the sound must spread out in every direction from the clap

items.q: Which is a suitable method for measuring the speed of ripples on a water surface?
items.correct: Use the dipper frequency and a measured wavelength in v = f λ
items.misconception: Measure the height of the ripples and divide it by the frequency
items.why: Big waves at sea look powerful and fast, and amplitude is linked to energy, so students connect amplitude to speed. The three wave quantities blur together. Speed depends on the medium, not on how tall the wave is. Only frequency and wavelength appear in v = f λ, and amplitude is measured on a different axis entirely.
items.random_wrong: Count the ripples reaching the far edge and multiply by the depth

items.q: Why is a stroboscope or a video recording often used when ripples are studied in a ripple tank?
items.correct: It freezes the pattern so wavelengths can be measured
items.misconception: It slows the ripples down so they really travel more slowly
items.why: Speed is first learned as distance divided by time, so students reach for a stopwatch. In a small tank the ripple crosses in a fraction of a second and is very hard to follow. A single ripple is faint, fast and hard to track. Freezing the pattern with a strobe or a video and measuring a wavelength, with the frequency read from the generator, is far more reliable.
items.random_wrong: It increases the frequency of the ripples on the water surface

items.q: (Physics only) A sound wave passes from air into water, where it travels faster. What happens to its frequency and its wavelength?
items.correct: The frequency stays the same and the wavelength becomes longer
items.misconception: The wavelength stays the same and the frequency increases
items.why: Students know something must change when the medium changes, and frequency is the quantity they think of first because pitch is the property they can hear. The source keeps sending the same number of waves each second, so f is unchanged and the pitch does not alter. With v = f λ and f fixed, a change in v forces a change in λ.
items.random_wrong: Both the frequency and the wavelength become larger

items.q: (Physics only) Sound travels faster in a steel rail than in air. When a sound passes from the air into the steel, which quantity is fixed by the source and cannot change?
items.correct: The frequency, which is set by the vibrating source
items.misconception: The wavelength, because the wave keeps its shape
items.why: Students know something must change when the medium changes, and frequency is the quantity they think of first because pitch is the property they can hear. The source keeps sending the same number of waves each second, so f is unchanged and the pitch does not alter. With v = f λ and f fixed, a change in v forces a change in λ.
items.random_wrong: The wave speed, which depends on the source's energy

items.q: In required practical activity 8, which apparatus is most suitable for measuring the wavelength of ripples in a ripple tank?
items.correct: A ruler placed under the projected ripple pattern
items.misconception: The frequency dial on the signal generator for the dipper
items.why: Repeating measurements is drilled as a general habit, so multiple-wavelength measurement is filed under 'repeats' rather than understood as a way of shrinking relative uncertainty. This is one measurement over a longer distance, not ten repeats. A 1 mm reading error on 20 mm is 5%; the same error on 200 mm is 0.5%.
items.random_wrong: A ruler measuring the height of a single ripple crest

items.q: In required practical activity 8, waves are also sent along a stretched string. Why is the distance across ten wavelengths measured and then divided by ten?
items.correct: It reduces the effect of uncertainty in each reading
items.misconception: One wavelength is far too small to be seen on a string
items.why: Repeating measurements is drilled as a general habit, so multiple-wavelength measurement is filed under 'repeats' rather than understood as a way of shrinking relative uncertainty. This is one measurement over a longer distance, not ten repeats. A 1 mm reading error on 20 mm is 5%; the same error on 200 mm is 0.5%.
items.random_wrong: The wavelength changes as the wave crosses the whole string

items.q: A diagram shows six complete waves. What is the frequency?
items.correct: The frequency cannot be read from the number of waves drawn; it is the number passing a point each second, which needs a time.
items.misconception: The frequency is six, because six waves are shown on the diagram.
items.why: Students are asked to count waves when finding a wavelength on a diagram, so counting becomes the default response, and a displacement–distance graph carries no time information at all. Check the horizontal axis. If it shows distance, the diagram gives wavelength, not frequency. Frequency needs waves counted against a clock, or a displacement–time graph.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the amplitude the same as the displacement?
items.correct: Amplitude is the maximum displacement from the undisturbed position, not the displacement at any chosen instant.
items.misconception: The amplitude is simply how far the point is from the centre line at the moment you look at it.
items.why: The two words are used loosely together, and on a diagram most points are somewhere between zero and maximum, so any of those distances looks like a candidate. Amplitude is one fixed value for the whole wave — the largest displacement reached. Displacement changes continuously as the point oscillates and is zero twice each cycle.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which axis is amplitude read on?
items.correct: On a displacement–distance graph, amplitude is read vertically on the displacement axis and wavelength horizontally on the distance axis.
items.misconception: Both amplitude and wavelength are measured horizontally along the wave.
items.why: Both are distances measured in metres, so students treat them as the same kind of measurement and reach for the horizontal axis, which is where wavelength was first shown to them. The two quantities live on different axes. Amplitude is how far a point moves from rest, read up the displacement axis; wavelength is how long one wave is, read along the distance axis.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How is [v = f λ] rearranged to find the wavelength?
items.correct: λ = v/f — divide the wave speed by the frequency.
items.misconception: Rearranging gives λ = v f, because the equation contains a multiplication.
items.why: Students see the multiplication sign in the original equation and keep it, changing which letters appear rather than changing the operation itself. To undo a multiplication you divide. Since v = f λ, dividing both sides by f gives λ = v/f, and a quick unit check confirms that m/s ÷ Hz gives metres.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What does the period of a wave measure?
items.correct: The period is the time taken for one complete wave to pass a point.
items.misconception: The period is the number of waves that pass a point each second.
items.why: Period and frequency are the two timing quantities and are defined side by side, so the definitions get swapped. Both sentences mention waves passing a point. Period is a time, measured in seconds; frequency is a count each second, measured in hertz. Read the unit off the answer to check which one has been described.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does sound slow down when it passes from air into water or steel?
items.correct: No — sound travels faster in liquids, and faster still in solids, than in air, so its wavelength gets longer.
items.misconception: Sound slows down in water and in solids because those materials are denser and harder to move through.
items.why: Students borrow the idea from light, which does slow in denser media, and from everyday experience of things being harder to push through water. Sound needs particles to pass the vibration on, and closely packed particles do this faster: about 340 m/s in air, 1500 m/s in water and 5000 m/s in steel.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In the echo method, why is the distance to the wall doubled?
items.correct: The sound travels to the wall and back before the echo is heard, so the path is twice the measured distance.
items.misconception: The sound travels faster on the way back, so the outward and return journeys must be treated differently.
items.why: An echo sounds different from the original clap — quieter and later — so students imagine the reflected sound is a changed wave rather than the same wave returning. Reflection changes the direction of the sound, not its speed; the medium is still air. The timed interval covers two equal journeys, so the distance used is 2 × the distance to the wall.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

specSource: AQA GCSE Physics (8463) specification; section 4.6.1.2 Waves in air, fluids and solids: Properties of waves
